event.name: Travel and Tourism Team Decision Making

sourceNotes: Seeded from TTDM roleplay performance indicators and hospitality and tourism cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: TTDM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the hospitality and tourism cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The per-leg charge a global distribution system bills an airline for every booked coupon, roughly $4 to $6 a segment, so a round trip with one connection each way costs the carrier four charges rather than one booking charge.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case asking why a carrier pushes travellers to its own site is answered by pricing the same itinerary through both channels — four segments at $5 is about $20 of distribution cost the direct booking does not incur.

terms.definition: A seat-allocation structure in which each fare bucket is a ceiling that includes every cheaper bucket beneath it, so selling one discount seat decrements availability in that bucket and in every higher bucket at once, and 9 seats in class Y does not mean 9 more seats on top of class Q's 4.
terms.whyItMatters: Revenue-management items hand a competitor an availability display and ask how many seats remain on the aircraft; adding the class counts together is the wrong answer because the buckets overlap.

terms.definition: A bonus percentage a supplier pays retroactively on an agency's whole year of bookings once a volume threshold is crossed, so an agency at $480,000 against a $500,000 tier earns not 10% but 13% on all of it the moment the last $20,000 books — making that final sale worth roughly $17,000 in commission, not $2,000.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM decision case about which supplier to steer a corporate account toward is decided by the retroactive tier, not by the headline base commission both suppliers quote.

terms.definition: A distribution arrangement in which the intermediary buys inventory at a supplier's wholesale price, sets its own retail price, and collects the traveller's full payment up front — keeping a spread of roughly 15 to 25% and holding the supplier's money until after the stay, where the alternative pays the intermediary 10 to 15% only after the supplier has been paid.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case weighing an online travel agency contract turns on both numbers — the wider spread and the delayed cash — not on the commission rate alone.

terms.definition: A distribution contract term barring a supplier from publishing a lower price on any other channel, including its own site; a narrow version restricts only public rates and leaves closed loyalty and mobile-app pricing free, while a wide version closes those too and has been struck down or banned in several jurisdictions.
terms.whyItMatters: When a TTDM roleplay asks how a hotel can undercut its own listing without breaching the agreement, the answer is the narrow-parity carve-out — a member-only rate behind a login — not a public discount.

terms.definition: The number of paying passengers a group must deliver to earn one free berth or seat, quoted as 15+1 or 20+1, whose cost the operator must spread across the payers — a complimentary place on a $1,200 tour adds $80 to each of 15 fares, or the group leader travels free only if the price already carries it.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM group-travel roleplay that offers a school a free chaperone place is scored on whether the team rebuilt the per-person price to absorb the comp rather than quoting the brochure rate and losing the margin.

terms.definition: The surcharge a solo traveller pays because tour and cruise prices are quoted per person on two people sharing, and a room's cost does not halve when only one guest occupies it — commonly 30 to 100% of the land portion, and near 100% where the operator has already contracted the room at a flat nightly rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM item asking what a solo client pays on a $2,400 per-person double-occupancy tour with a 60% supplement wants $3,840, and the supplement applies only to the land component when air is priced separately.

terms.definition: The passenger count at which a scheduled departure's fixed costs — coach charter, guide, escort, and any complimentary places — are finally covered by per-person contribution, and the number below which an operator cancels rather than operates: $4,500 of fixed cost against $300 of contribution per traveller cancels below 15.
terms.whyItMatters: TTDM cases about whether to run or consolidate a thin departure are decided by this count and the cancellation deadline in the brochure, not by whether the departure shows a headline loss.

terms.definition: A cruise capacity measure whose denominator counts two guests per cabin regardless of how many the cabin sleeps, so filling third and fourth berths pushes the figure above 100% — a ship reported at 105% is full and carrying extra guests, not overbooked.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM competitor handed a cruise line's 104% occupancy must read it as upper-berth fill driving onboard spend, and not describe it as an oversell problem the way a hotel figure over 100% would be.

terms.definition: Fare divided by nights on a double-occupancy basis, the only figure that compares itineraries of different lengths — a $1,400 seven-night sailing at $200 a night is more expensive than a $1,800 ten-night at $180, even though the headline fare says otherwise, and port charges and taxes are normally excluded from it.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM roleplay asking a team to justify a recommendation between two sailings is won on this per-night number plus what is excluded from it, not on the total fare the client first sees.

terms.definition: A percentage levied on room revenue for stays under a statutory length — commonly 28 or 30 consecutive nights, past which the guest becomes a resident and the tax stops — collected by the property on top of any sales tax and remitted to the local government, so a $200 room in a jurisdiction charging 9% lodging plus 7% sales bills $232.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case on extended-stay pricing or on where a destination's marketing budget comes from needs both the stacking of the two taxes and the night threshold that ends the lodging one.

terms.definition: A self-assessment scheme in which lodging properties in a defined boundary vote to charge themselves a fixed percentage of each room night — typically 1 to 2% — to fund destination marketing, adopted only on petition of owners representing more than half the assessed revenue and renewable for a set term.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case asking how a destination funds a campaign without a public tax vote turns on this petition threshold and on the fact that the assessment is the hotels' own money, which is why they demand the campaign's room-night return.

terms.definition: The proportion of a cooperative campaign a destination organization will cover against partner money, written as grant to partner — a 1:2 offer capped at $30,000 means the partner must spend $60,000 to draw the full grant and the campaign carries $90,000, and partner spend below the cap scales the grant down rather than forfeiting it.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM co-op marketing roleplay is scored on sizing the partner contribution the ratio demands and on stating the cap, because a team that budgets only the grant funds a third of the campaign it just promised.

terms.definition: Campaign spend divided by the incremental room nights it can be shown to have caused — $200,000 against 4,000 attributable nights is $50 a night — which is judged against the lodging tax and assessment those nights yield, so a $50 cost on a $180 room paying 9% tax returns about $16 and fails.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case defending a destination marketing budget to a hotel board must compare this figure with the tax yield per room night, and must use incremental nights rather than every night booked during the flight.

terms.definition: The factor converting visitor spending into total economic output by adding indirect supplier purchases and induced household spending to the direct amount — a coefficient of 1.6 turns $1,000,000 of visitor spend into $1,600,000 of output, and the figure is a regional estimate that shrinks as more supplies are imported.
terms.whyItMatters: TTDM economic-impact cases hand a team an arrivals count, an average spend and a coefficient and expect the total impact computed, plus the caution that the coefficient is not transferable between destinations.

terms.definition: The share of visitor spending that leaves the host economy immediately — imported food and fuel, foreign-owned hotel profit sent home, and fares paid to non-local carriers — reaching 70 to 80% in small island destinations, so $10,000,000 of arrivals spending may retain only $2,000,000 locally before any multiplier is applied.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case arguing for local sourcing or community-based operators is built on this percentage; quoting gross visitor spending as the community benefit is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: The per-visit contribution of a same-day visitor, typically a quarter to a third of an overnight guest's because it carries no room charge and therefore no lodging tax at all — 50,000 day visitors at $75 can be worth less to the destination's marketing fund than 10,000 overnight visitors at $250 across two nights.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM festival or attraction case that reports huge attendance must convert it into overnight equivalents before claiming a lodging-tax return, because the funding the campaign is defended by comes only from rooms.

terms.definition: The statutory ceiling on what a carrier owes for lost or damaged luggage, set per passenger in dollars on US domestic itineraries and in Special Drawing Rights — a fluctuating IMF unit, not dollars — under the Montreal Convention internationally, with anything above it recoverable only if excess value was declared and paid for at check-in.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM claim roleplay for a client whose $4,000 of equipment vanished turns on which regime the itinerary fell under and whether excess valuation was purchased, not on the replacement cost the client quotes.

terms.definition: A visa-free limit allowing 90 days of stay inside the zone within any rolling 180-day window, counted backwards from each day present rather than reset by a single exit — so a traveller who used 60 days in the last four months has 30 left today, and every day of an old stay only frees up once it falls outside the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM itinerary-planning roleplay for a client returning to Europe within months is answered by counting the rolling window; treating a trip home as a reset is what produces a refused entry at the border.

terms.definition: An entry requirement, common across Asia, the Middle East and parts of Latin America, that a passport remain valid for six months beyond the arrival date — so a document expiring in four months is refused for a trip departing next week even though it has not yet expired, and airlines are fined for boarding the passenger.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM booking roleplay must check the expiry date against the return date plus six months before ticketing; the client is turned away at check-in, not at the border, and the agency wears the rebooking.

terms.definition: A surety bond or trust account a travel seller must post to register in states such as California, Florida, Washington and Hawaii, sized in the tens of thousands of dollars and paired in some states with a consumer restitution fund fee per transaction, so client deposits are protected if the seller fails before departure.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM case on opening an agency across state lines is scored on naming the registration and the client-funds protection; an unregistered seller taking deposits in those states is committing an offence, not an oversight.

terms.definition: The alphanumeric string attached to a ticketed fare that encodes its conditions — the booking class letter first, then markers for season, weekday or weekend travel, advance purchase in days, minimum stay, and refundability — so two passengers in the same cabin can hold completely different change rights.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM roleplay asking whether a client may move a flight is answered by reading this code's restriction markers, not by the cabin the client is sitting in.

terms.definition: A cruise booking sold by category only, with no stateroom number assigned until close to sailing, priced below the lowest published fare in that category in exchange for the line keeping the right to place the guest anywhere at or above it.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM client who wants a discount but insists on a specific deck cannot be sold one, and the trade-off — cheaper, possible free upgrade, no location control, often no cancellation flexibility — is what the judge expects explained.

terms.definition: A US Department of Transportation requirement that the first price shown for air travel include every mandatory tax and government fee, so a carrier may not advertise a base fare and add unavoidable charges later — optional charges such as checked bags may still be added, but must be disclosed.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM promotion roleplay writing a fare advertisement is scored on quoting the all-in figure; splitting out mandatory taxes to make the headline number smaller is the violation the judge is looking for.

terms.definition: Giving up a seat on an oversold flight in exchange for negotiated compensation the passenger accepts — usually a voucher, sometimes cash, plus a confirmed later seat — which is not capped by regulation and is not owed at all, unlike the statutory payment for a passenger removed against their will.
terms.whyItMatters: A TTDM roleplay coaching a client at an oversold gate depends on knowing that accepting the offer converts a legal entitlement into whatever was negotiated, so the counter-offer has to be made before agreeing.

terms.definition: Moore's gap between the 13.5% early-adopter band, which buys on the promise of a breakthrough and tolerates an incomplete product, and the 34% early majority, which buys only on references from people already like themselves; products stall in it because the two groups will not act as references for each other, and the standard bridge is dominating one narrow beachhead segment until its references become credible to the next group.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay shows strong early sales that suddenly flatten, naming this gap and the beachhead fix is the diagnosis a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Takes last period's actual as next period's number and nothing else, and exists to be the benchmark: compute its error first, and any model whose MAPE is not meaningfully below that baseline is not paying for the effort it costs, however advanced the technique behind it sounds.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which forecasting approach a firm should keep; the defensible answer is whichever one beats the zero-effort baseline by a measured margin, and a plan that cannot show that improvement loses the argument for its forecasting spend.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: A Title VII theory attacking a facially neutral policy — a lifting test, a degree requirement, a credit check — that screens out a protected group at a substantially lower rate, with no proof of intent needed. Federal selection guidelines flag a rate below four-fifths of the highest group's, after which the employer must show the practice is job-related and consistent with business necessity. Its neighbour, disparate treatment, requires showing intentional differential treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: Hiring roleplays about a strength requirement that eliminates most female applicants are argued under this theory, not under intentional discrimination.

terms.definition: The number-two or number-three firm by share — roughly 30% against a leader's 40% in Kotler's benchmark structure, above a follower's 20% and a nicher's 10% — which attacks the leader or smaller rivals head-on rather than imitating; a firm with the same share that deliberately copies the leader and avoids provoking retaliation is a follower, so the label is set by chosen posture, not by size alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Strategy roleplays that hand you a share table expect the four positions named and the posture defended; calling every non-leader a competitor loses the distinction.

terms.definition: The number of weeks it takes a campaign's carried-over effect to fall to 50% of its starting level, computed from the weekly retention rate as ln(0.5) ÷ ln(rate) — a rate of 0.7 gives about 1.9 weeks — so a short half-life forces flights roughly monthly while a long one permits long gaps between bursts.
terms.whyItMatters: Flighting-versus-continuity items expect the weeks figure computed, not a description of the trade-off, and the same number sets the measurement window a plan claims when it attributes sales to a campaign.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: Petty and Cacioppo's two-route account of persuasion. An audience with both the motivation and the ability to think takes the central route, where argument quality decides and the resulting attitude is durable and resists counter-argument. An audience missing either one takes the peripheral route, where source attractiveness, the sheer length of the list and mood decide, and the attitude fades quickly. Adding more evidence for a distracted, uninvolved audience therefore changes nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A persuasive-message item that asks why a detailed cost-savings memo convinced the CFO but not the frontline staff is asking which route each audience was on.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: The distance between the top-down number corporate assumes and the sum of the territory-level bottom-up forecasts, stated as a percentage of the top-down total; a gap past roughly 5% has to be closed by named actions with volume attached to each before the plan is approved, never by splitting the difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-approval scenarios hand a corporate target and the field's rolled-up total and expect the gap quantified and assigned; the judge's follow-up is always which specific actions close it and what each is worth.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: The spending level on a diminishing-returns response curve where the last dollar invested returns exactly one dollar of contribution; below it more spending still adds profit, above it volume keeps climbing while profit falls, so the stopping test is marginal contribution per marginal dollar equal to 1.0 — not whether total return is still positive.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget items deliberately show total return positive at every spending level to see whether the competitor stops at the marginal break-even; a plan arguing for more spend past that point is refuted with its own numbers.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: Leading by modeling integrity, fairness, and moral principles.
terms.whyItMatters: It builds organizational trust and sets the tone for employee behavior.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: The percentage volume increase a discount must produce merely to hold contribution flat: discount per unit ÷ (normal contribution per unit − discount per unit). A $1 cut against $4 of unit contribution needs 33% more units; a $2 cut against the same $4 needs 100%, which is why deep cuts almost never pay for themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-approval questions give margin and discount depth and expect the required lift computed and compared with the forecast lift; anything forecast below the break-even figure is a promotion the plan should reject.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: Loan amount divided by the appraised value of the asset securing it; the higher it is, the less cushion a lender has and the more likely mortgage insurance is required.
terms.whyItMatters: Home-financing scenarios test why a larger down payment lowers the cost of borrowing, and this ratio is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: Period sales divided by that period's seasonal index — 130,000 units in a month carrying an index of 1.30 is 100,000 on a level basis — and any trend line must be fitted to these adjusted figures, because fitting a line straight to raw seasonal data reads the busy season as growth that is not there.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast items hand monthly actuals alongside indexes and expect the adjusted series produced before any projection; skipping the division is the standard error that inflates a plan's growth claim and gets caught on the follow-up.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: Technology that stores and manages employee data and HR processes.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRIS improves efficiency and enables data-driven HR decisions.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: Divides a town's retail sales per resident by the state's retail sales per resident: 1.00 means locals spend exactly the statewide average at home, above 1.00 means the town is pulling shoppers in from outside its borders, and 0.80 means a fifth of local buying power is leaking to other towns.
terms.whyItMatters: Trading-area and site questions give local and statewide sales per person and expect the ratio plus a read on leakage; it is the figure behind arguing that a market is under-served and can support another store.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: The 1,024-based unit an operating system counts in, set against the 1,000-based unit a drive is sold in: a '1 TB' disk holds 10^12 bytes, but the OS divides by 1,024 three times and reports 931 GB — a 7% shortfall that widens at every prefix step, so a 4 TB drive shows as 3.64 TB, roughly 9% short.
terms.whyItMatters: A records-storage item asks how many years of files a purchased drive really holds; sizing the archive off the number on the box overstates capacity before the first backup runs.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: Compares an industry's share of local employment or sales with its share nationally — local share ÷ national share — so 1.0 marks a perfectly typical market, above about 1.25 says the activity is concentrated here and likely serves customers beyond it, and below about 0.75 says local demand is being met from somewhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: Situation-analysis questions supply local and national employment figures and expect the ratio read against 1.0; it is how a plan defends choosing one metro over another with evidence rather than preference.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: Planning, executing, and monitoring work to hit objectives within time and budget.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets managers coordinate resources and deliver on schedule.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: Degree program alternating full-time paid work terms with academic terms, where the work terms carry academic credit and a faculty evaluation. An internship is a single standalone placement with no required academic component, which is why students on this track often graduate with a year or more of documented, evaluated experience.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to build work experience while still in school is scored on distinguishing the credit-bearing alternating program from a one-off summer job.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: The count of subordinates reporting directly to one manager; a wide span (roughly 10 or more) flattens the hierarchy, cuts management layers and cost, and demands more delegation, while a narrow span (3 to 5) builds a tall structure with closer supervision and slower decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Management exam items hand you a headcount and a layer count and ask for the average span or for which structure results, so the ratio has to be computed rather than described.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: A short-window, fixed-dollar bonus paid per unit on one targeted product — $50 a unit for 30 days, frequently funded by the manufacturer and paid outside the regular commission plan. An accelerator instead lifts the commission percentage on everything sold past quota, so one steers which item gets pushed and the other rewards total volume.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selling items describe a vendor paying a retailer's floor staff per unit and ask what the payment is; a promotion roleplay expects you to name the mechanism that redirects selling effort to one slow-moving SKU.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: The price one division charges another inside the same company, which shifts reported profit between units and, across borders, between tax jurisdictions. Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code requires it to meet the arm's-length standard - the price unrelated parties would have agreed on - so a firm cannot simply invoice its own subsidiary at cost or at zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business roleplays ask why one division's results look poor while the company's consolidated profit is healthy, and the internal price is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: The deadline for filing a claim, running from when the cause of action accrued and varying by claim type — commonly two to three years for personal injury, four years for a sale of goods under the UCC, and longer for written contracts. A discovery rule can delay the start until the harm was or should have been found, and tolling pauses the clock during a plaintiff's minority or a defendant's absence from the state.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-procedure questions ask whether a customer injured three years ago can still bring suit against the business.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Models trustworthiness as credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation — so visibly acting in your own interest divides away everything the other three terms earn. Credibility is about words, reliability about repeated actions over time, and intimacy about safety in disclosure, which is why a person can be believable and still not be trusted.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on rebuilding a client or coworker relationship is scored on lowering the self-orientation term — leading with their problem — rather than on producing more credentials.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: The total amount, including interest and fees, paid to borrow money.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing the true cost of credit lets competitors judge whether borrowing is worthwhile.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: The right of a worker leaving an employer with 20 or more employees to keep the group health plan for up to 18 months, extended to 29 months for disability and 36 months for a spouse or dependent after divorce or death. The qualified beneficiary has 60 days to elect and may be charged 102% of the full premium — the employer subsidy ends, which is why the monthly cost often quadruples.
terms.whyItMatters: A separation roleplay is scored on stating the election window and that the former employee now pays the full premium plus the 2% administrative charge.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: A spreadsheet address locking exactly one of the two coordinates — $B5 pins the column and lets the row travel, B$5 does the reverse. Filling a multiplication grid both across and down needs one of each inside the same formula ($B5*C$4); pinning both coordinates or neither returns a wrong value in every cell except the one it was typed into.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items grade the filled grid rather than the first cell, so a formula that is correct where it is written and wrong everywhere it is dragged scores zero.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days, plus safety stock — the on-hand level that triggers a replenishment order, so it answers WHEN to order while economic order quantity answers HOW MUCH.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you daily usage, a supplier lead time and a buffer and ask at what stock level a buyer should place the reorder; picking the order size instead of the trigger level is the standard wrong answer.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Planning credential CFP Board grants to a candidate who holds a bachelor's degree, completes registered coursework, passes a 170-question exam given in two three-hour sessions, and logs 6,000 hours of professional experience — or 4,000 hours under a supervised apprenticeship — then renews with 30 continuing-education hours every two years, 2 of them CFP Board ethics. Against a licence that only obliges a recommendation to be suitable, the difference is the standard of care: the holder must act as a fiduciary and place the client's interest ahead of their own whenever advice is given.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance roleplays that make a competitor explain designations to a client reward the fiduciary-versus-suitability line, and exam items on ongoing education use the 30-hour, two-year renewal as the tested number.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: A capability that passes the Prahalad-and-Hamel three-part test — it opens access to multiple markets, contributes visibly to perceived customer benefit, and is hard for rivals to imitate; a strength failing any one of the three is merely a capability and not a basis for strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items list four company strengths and ask which qualifies as a core competency, and the wrong answers are strengths that fail exactly one leg of the test.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.
